hero.placement: post header through the logo front-matter field
hero.visual_goal: Introduce the tutorial through shopper approval, UCP communication and a merchant-confirmed order, matching the journal's opening artwork.
hero.prompt: Use case: illustration-story. Create a polished 16:9 landscape hero illustration for a beginner's tutorial on Universal Commerce Protocol. This is the opening artwork for a technical commerce journal, not an official protocol logo. Match a friendly business explainer illustration: pale blue-white background, crisp dark navy outlines, flat vector-like cartoon forms, minimal shading, disciplined blue, teal, green and muted orange accents, generous whitespace. Show one coherent left-to-right purchase scene. On the left a shopper holds a smartphone with a large moss-green outdoor jacket product thumbnail and a clearly visible green approval check. A small speech bubble near the shopper reads 'Approve'. In the center, an elegant large connector or short bridge labeled exactly 'UCP' links the shopping application's rounded interface panel to a merchant storefront. Two clean parallel communication lines cross this bridge in opposite directions, conveying request and response. On the right, a welcoming small blue-and-teal merchant storefront with a green jacket in the window, a simple order document with a green check, and a small sealed orange parcel beside it. Above the order document the only label is 'Order'. The merchant should feel like the source of the order; the phone shows the shopper's approval. Keep the composition balanced and immediately understandable, with large simple shapes readable as a page header and no content near the edges. Text is limited to exactly 'Approve', 'UCP', and 'Order'; no article title, subtitle, dates, brand names, official brand marks, card numbers, dense code, robot, or tiny labels. Opaque light background, no border or watermark.
hero.inspection: Checked readable labels, opposite request/response arrows, shopper approval and merchant order, and consistency with the journal's blue, teal, green and orange palette.

figures.visual_goal: Show that UCP connects the shopping application to the merchant, while the merchant retains its commerce systems and payment processing.
figures.prompt: Create an accurate editorial explainer diagram for a beginner's Universal Commerce Protocol tutorial, 16:9 landscape. Warm ivory background, dark forest green typography, teal and muted amber accents, crisp flat vector-like shapes, very readable large labels, generous whitespace. Six nodes: top row left to right 'Shopper', 'Shopping app', 'Merchant'; below Shopping app 'Wallet'; below Merchant two small nodes 'Commerce systems' and 'Payment provider'. Use simple person, app window, shop, wallet, database and payment icons. Exactly these directed arrows with short labels: Shopper to Shopping app 'Approves purchase'; Shopping app to Merchant 'UCP requests'; Merchant to Shopping app 'Quotes and status'; Wallet to Shopping app 'Payment token'; Merchant to Commerce systems 'Checks and records'; Merchant to Payment provider 'Processes payment'. Route arrows without overlaps. No arrow that suggests the wallet transfers money through the app. No logos, no title, no decorative characters, no dense text.
figures.alt: A shopper approves a purchase in an application. The application exchanges UCP requests and status with the merchant, receives a payment token from a wallet, and the merchant calls its commerce systems and payment provider.
figures.caption: UCP connects the application to the merchant; the merchant still checks its records and processes the purchase.

figures.visual_goal: Explain that only mutually supported, version-compatible capabilities can be used, and extensions depend on their parent capability.
figures.prompt: Create an accurate 16:9 educational diagram with warm ivory background, dark forest green typography, teal and muted amber, clean flat vector-like cards, generous whitespace, no title or logos. Top left card labeled 'Merchant supports' containing three rows 'Checkout', 'Shipping', 'Loyalty'. Top right card labeled 'App supports' containing three rows 'Checkout', 'Shipping', 'Discounts'. Two arrows from top cards to a centered bottom card, each labeled 'Compare versions'. Bottom card labeled 'Agreed features' containing exactly two large badges 'Checkout' and 'Shipping'. Under the Shipping badge small readable text 'Extends checkout'. Show Loyalty and Discounts in gray in their original cards, not in the agreed card. Bottom footnote 'Matching features and versions'. Use seven distinct capability badges in the top area and bottom two as needed, but preserve this exact logic. No Venn diagram, no code, no extra feature, no decorative people.
figures.alt: The merchant offers checkout, shipping and loyalty, while the application offers checkout, shipping and discounts. Their agreement includes checkout and shipping when the versions match; shipping depends on checkout.
figures.caption: A feature is usable only when both participants support a compatible version and its required parent capability. Shipping here is provided by the fulfillment extension.

figures.visual_goal: Separate missing information, readiness, processing and a confirmed order, with human handoff as a supported branch.
figures.prompt: Create a simplified conceptual flow diagram, 16:9 landscape, warm ivory, forest green, teal and amber palette, large readable text, clean flat cards. Main horizontal row of four boxes labeled exactly 'Missing details', 'Ready to complete', 'Processing', 'Order placed'. Arrows between adjacent main boxes labeled respectively 'Provide details', 'Confirm purchase', 'Completion succeeds'. Fifth box below first two labeled 'Buyer handoff', with arrow from Missing details to Buyer handoff labeled 'Human needed', and a return arrow from Buyer handoff to Missing details labeled 'Check latest state'. Sixth separate note card bottom right labeled 'Canceled or expired' with small text 'Stop this checkout'. No arrows from canceled card. Add short note under Processing 'Wait or check status'. This is a simplified teaching flow, not a complete state machine; do not add alternative transitions. No code status strings, no logos, no title, no extra words or decorative people.
figures.alt: A simplified checkout flow moves from missing details to ready to complete, processing and order placed. A buyer handoff can resolve information the application cannot provide. Canceled or expired sessions must stop.
figures.caption: Readiness permits an attempt; processing means wait; only a completed checkout confirms the order. This diagram simplifies the full lifecycle.

figures.placement: after the wallet and token explanation
figures.visual_goal: Show the separation between shopper approval, credential creation, and merchant-side payment processing.
figures.prompt: Create a 16:9 landscape educational payment diagram, clean flat vector-like style, warm ivory background, forest green labels, teal token arrows, muted amber approval arrows. Five nodes only: top left 'Shopper', top center 'Wallet', bottom center 'Shopping app', bottom right 'Merchant', top right 'Payment provider'. Arrows exactly: Shopper to Wallet 'Approve'; Wallet down to Shopping app 'Token'; Shopping app right to Merchant 'Token with request'; Merchant up to Payment provider 'Process'; Payment provider down to Merchant 'Result'. Separate the two parallel merchant/payment arrows clearly. Include a tiny locked-card icon inside Wallet, but no card numbers anywhere. Bottom note in large readable type 'A token is not an order confirmation'. Do not show money flowing through Shopping app. No logos, no title, no extra arrows, no claim that AP2 processes money.
figures.alt: The shopper approves a wallet interaction. The wallet supplies a token to the shopping application, which sends it to the merchant. The merchant processes payment with its provider and receives the result.
figures.caption: The application carries the agreed credential; the merchant's payment integration determines the payment result.

figures.placement: after the lost completion response scenario
figures.visual_goal: Teach that a lost response creates uncertainty and that retrieving the existing checkout can recover the same order without a second purchase.
figures.prompt: Create an accurate 16:9 landscape sequence illustration for a beginner's commerce tutorial. Warm ivory background, forest green headings, teal arrows, amber warning, crisp vector-like style with large readable text. Two columns headed 'Shopping app' on left and 'Merchant' on right, each with a vertical thin lifeline. Four sequential messages top to bottom: left to right solid arrow 'Complete checkout'; right to left dashed arrow broken by a small amber X labeled 'Response lost'; left to right solid arrow 'Get checkout'; right to left solid arrow 'Completed: same order'. Beside merchant after first message show a small document card labeled 'One order'. Beside app after lost response show small amber label 'Outcome unknown'. Footer note 'Check state before retrying'. No second order, no second payment, no automatic retry arrow, no code, no logos, no title. Make message directions unmistakable and do not cross labels with arrows.
figures.alt: The application asks the merchant to complete checkout. The merchant creates one order, but the response is lost. The application retrieves that checkout and receives confirmation of the same order.
figures.caption: Losing the response does not undo the purchase. Retrieve the existing checkout before deciding whether a retry is necessary.

A second teal arrow runs from that card to a right card labelled 'Checkout' with a clipboard icon. figures.alt: A jacket product offers sizes S, M and L. The medium size leads to the variant identifier ridgewalker-w-m-moss, which goes into checkout. A crossed-out path shows the parent product is not used directly.
